citation.title: Data-driven topology optimization of spinodoid metamaterials with seamlessly tunable anisotropy
citation.authors: Li Zheng, Siddhant Kumar, Dennis M. Kochmann
citation.venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 383, 113894
citation.version_coded: Version of record (CC BY 4.0 copy from the TU Delft repository; journal pagination used in locators), cross-checked against arXiv v2 (19 May 2021) HTML

included.reason: I-SPEED (screening code confirmed at full text; comparator is FE homogenization inside FE²-type two-scale TO)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The trained DNN surrogate returns a spinodoid RVE's homogenized stiffness in about 0.001 s per sample, versus roughly 5 min for FE homogenization, so stiffness evaluations inside the two-scale optimization become orders of magnitude cheaper.
claim.key_phrase: accurate stiffness predictions instantly compared to several minutes for FEM-based homogenization
claim.location: Section 4.1, p. 11 (first comparison with a classical method in the main text; abstract, conclusion and introduction hold only qualitative claims); numbers in Appendix B, Table B.1, p. 23
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Derived by coder, not stated: Table B.1 FE homogenization 5 min (300 s, 16 MPI cores) ÷ DNN prediction 0.001 s (one sample, one CPU, no parallelization) = 300,000 per stiffness evaluation. The paper gives only an orders-of-magnitude statement and calls the runtimes a qualitative measure (Appendix B). This is not an optimization-level speed-up: no classical FE² or SIMP optimization runtime is reported.
claim.alternatives: (1) Quality vs single-scale SIMP (solid isotropic material, p = 4): Benchmark I spinodoid 5.602×10⁻¹ vs SIMP 5.299×10⁻¹ (spinodoid higher, 5.7% [derived]; Fig. 7c); II 2.282×10¹ vs 2.490×10¹, 8.35% lower (Fig. 10c); III 8.297×10¹ vs 8.723×10¹, 4.88% lower (Fig. 12c); IV 7.8×10³ vs 7.9×10³, 1.27% lower, flagged by the authors as possibly a numerical artefact (Section 5.4, Fig. 14c). (2) Qualitative: abstract (costly homogenization replaced by an accurate, efficient surrogate); conclusion (calculations sped up significantly; advantages over classical SIMP from the enlarged design space); Section 4.2 (AD sensitivities avoid FE-based numerical differentiation).

baseline.classical_method: FE computational homogenization of each spinodoid RVE (the step FE²-type concurrent two-scale TO repeats per element and iteration); single-scale SIMP (p = 4) as design-quality reference (Section 5.2)
baseline.implementation: Homogenization: in-house C++ FEM code (Table B.1). SIMP reference: not stated. ML side: PyTorch in Python; TO in Python with IPOPT (Section 3.1, Table B.1)
baseline.solver: not stated (homogenization and macroscale FE); optimizer IPOPT interior-point (Section 3.1)
baseline.hardware_classical: Euler IV cluster (ETH Zürich), two 18-core 2.7 GHz Intel Xeon Gold 6150, 192 GB; 16 MPI cores for FE homogenization (Table B.1, footnote c)
baseline.hardware_ml: DNN prediction and training: four 12-core 2.2 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2650, 256 GB, CPU without parallelization (Table B.1, footnote b); TO benchmarks: Euler IV CPU without parallelization (footnote c)
baseline.problem_size: RVE mesh not stated in this article. Macroscale: Benchmark I 64×48×2 tetrahedral grid; II 22,060 tetrahedra (110,300 design variables); III 25,350 (126,750); IV 48,000 (240,000) (Sections 5.2–5.4)
baseline.classical_iterations: not applicable to one RVE homogenization (six load cases per RVE, Section 2.2); SIMP reference iteration count and stopping rule not stated
baseline.classical_time: around 5 min per FE homogenization (Table B.1; Appendix B, p. 23); minutes-scale in Section 4.1; no classical TO runtime reported
baseline.ml_time: 0.001 s per DNN stiffness prediction, one sample (Table B.1); full surrogate-based TO runs: Benchmark I 3 h, II 3.5 h, III 4.5 h, IV 8 h (Table B.1)
baseline.training_time: 10 min, PyTorch on CPU without parallelization (Table B.1); data and training adapted from Kumar et al. 2020a (Table B.1 note)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated as a total; 19,170 training + 2,130 test FE-homogenized samples (Section 5.1) at about 5 min each (Table B.1) [inferred total: 21,300 × 5 min ≈ 1,775 h on 16 cores]; data reused from Kumar et al. 2020a
baseline.quality_metric: Surrogate: R² vs FEM on 2,130 test samples (stiffness R² ≥ 0.996; AD sensitivities vs central FD R² ≥ 0.999) (Section 5.1, Figs. 5–6). Designs: optimized compliance vs single-scale SIMP (Figs. 7c, 10c, 12c, 14c)
baseline.quality_gap: Benchmark I: 5.602×10⁻¹ (spinodoid) vs 5.299×10⁻¹ (SIMP), spinodoid 5.7% higher [derived]; II: 2.282×10¹ vs 2.490×10¹ (8.35% lower); III: 8.297×10¹ vs 8.723×10¹ (4.88% lower); IV: 7.8×10³ vs 7.9×10³ (1.27% lower) (Figs. 7c, 10c, 12c, 14c)

R1.evidence: The primary outcome is a per-evaluation comparison (Section 4.1, p. 11; Table B.1, p. 23), and at that level the DNN output is checked against the same FE homogenization it replaces: R² ≥ 0.996 for every stiffness component on 2,130 held-out FEM samples, and R² ≥ 0.999 for the AD sensitivities against central differences of FEM stiffnesses (Section 5.1, p. 12, Figs. 5-6). The speed comparison therefore sits within the ML method's reported error of the classical result. No fail condition holds: a quality comparison exists and the DNN output is not shown to be worse than its reported error. The unstated RVE mesh ('for the meshes used in our study', p. 11) and the authors' remark that the runtimes are only a qualitative measure (Appendix B, p. 23) concern the baseline's cost and the timing protocol, not quality matching. No FE²-type optimization is run, so there is no design-level speed claim to match. Unsure → pass.

R2.evidence: Table B.1: FE homogenization uses an in-house C++ FEM code on 16 MPI cores (Euler IV), while the DNN runs on one CPU without parallelization. No GPU is used, so (c) does not apply; the abstract gives no baseline figure (b); no fixed iteration count applies (d). Solver type and RVE mesh are not stated; no inefficiency is evident. Unsure → pass.

R3.evidence: Table B.1 (p. 23): DNN training 10 min; FE homogenization about 5 min per sample. Section 5.1 (p. 12): 19,170 training + 2,130 test samples. The total data-generation cost is never stated [inferred ≈1,775 h of 16-core time], and data and training were reused from Kumar et al. 2020a (Table B.1 note). No break-even is given. Appendix B frames the gain per prediction, but the conclusion's speed-up statement is not limited to per-query use (Section 6, pp. 20-21).

R4.evidence: Surrogate outputs are checked against FEM on 2,130 held-out samples (Section 5.1). The optimized compliances of the returned designs (Figs. 7c, 10c, 12c, 14c) are computed with DNN-predicted stiffness; no FE homogenization or fully resolved FE re-check of the final design parameters is reported [inferred from Sections 3–5 and Appendix A], and the achieved relative density is not reported. Partial because the macroscale FE is real and the surrogate is independently validated; a stricter reading (design performance rests on the surrogate) gives fail.

reporting.n_test_cases: 4 benchmark problems (Sections 5.2–5.4); Benchmarks II and III each also at 5 mesh resolutions (Figs. 10c, 12c); surrogate test set of 2,130 samples (Section 5.1)

notes: Stratum is a judgment call. The only ML-vs-classical speed comparison is per stiffness evaluation (DNN vs FE homogenization), used here as a cost proxy for FE²-type two-scale optimization; no optimization-level runtime of a classical method is reported. If the verifier rejects this proxy, the primary outcome becomes the compliance comparison with single-scale SIMP (quality stratum; see alternatives), where Benchmark I is worse than SIMP and the design-space difference (multiscale vs solid material), not the ML, drives the gains [inferred]. The arXiv v2 HTML rendering omits the Table B.1 cells, so the version of record was used. No code or data statement in the article. Adjudicator check (2026-09-24): read the version of record (final published version, CC BY) from the TU Delft repository (resolver.tudelft.nl/uuid:5677e89a-7496-4c8f-bf9c-101a94fe4832, listed by OpenAlex) and the arXiv v2 PDF; the passages used here (Sec. 4.1, p. 11; Sec. 5.1, p. 12; conclusion, pp. 20-21; Table B.1 and Appendix B, p. 23) agree in both versions. The version of record has a competing-interest declaration but no code or data statement.

R1.reason: The primary outcome is per stiffness evaluation, and the DNN is validated against the same FE homogenization it replaces (R² ≥ 0.996 per component on 2,130 held-out samples, Sec. 5.1, p. 12), so the comparison sits within the ML method's reported error of the classical result (§5.3 R1 pass). The first coder's reasons (no FE² run, unstated RVE mesh, runtimes called qualitative, App. B, p. 23) concern the claim's scope, the baseline's cost and the timing protocol rather than quality matching; unsure means pass.

R3.reason: Training cost is reported (10 min, Table B.1, p. 23), but the cost of generating the 21,300 FEM-labelled samples (Sec. 5.1, p. 12) is never stated; it can only be inferred by multiplying the counts by the 5-min per-evaluation time, and the data were adapted from Kumar et al. 2020a (Table B.1 note). That is the §5.3 R3 partial case (data-generation cost missing), whatever the reading of the per-prediction footnote, and no break-even is given.
